# Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author

Source: https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-14 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At a few hundred people, founders make a small fraction of decisions, managers inherit precedents from people they never met, and turnover is constant. The decision record's job becomes delegation: formal decision classes, a precedent slot, standard handover packs and a first calibration, without sliding into compliance theatre.

At a few hundred people, founders make a small fraction of the decisions. Managers make most of them, many managers have never met the people whose decisions they inherit, and turnover becomes constant. The enterprise brain's job becomes delegation: letting good reasoning travel. Four things do that: formal decision classes, a precedent slot before each decision, a standard handover pack, and a first calibration in one high-volume class. The trap is compliance theatre.

This is the fourth rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The previous rung, [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/), dealt with shared meaning. At two hundred, the problem is delegation.

## What delegation breaks

Growth introduces a middle layer. Decisions that a founder once made in a minute, with full context, are now made by a team lead with partial context, often following a precedent set by someone who has since left. The organisation is making more decisions than ever, and each one is made with less of the history behind it.

Turnover makes this routine rather than occasional. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported median tenure with the current employer of 4.1 years in January 2026, and 3.9 years in the private sector. In a firm of two hundred, people change roles or leave most months, and every move takes reasons with it. Our piece [*Handovers are where reasoning pours out*](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) describes the mechanism.

The result is inconsistency that nobody sees until someone measures it. Daniel Kahneman and colleagues described the method in *Harvard Business Review* in October 2016 as a noise audit: several professionals in the same role assess the same cases, and the spread of their answers measures the noise. In one audit at an insurer, as reported by Insurance Thought Leadership, executives expected about a 10% difference between the high and low quotes their 48 underwriters set on the same case. The typical difference was 55%.

This is also the first stage at which some decision classes become frequent enough to learn from. Sales deals, support escalations, hiring decisions and discount approvals each run into the hundreds a year.

> The organisation is making more decisions than ever, and each one is made with less of the history behind it.

## Decision classes, formally

Define the recurring classes properly now. For each: the owner, the template, the needs list (what a good decision in this class requires), and the falsifier convention. A discount approval should look the same wherever in the company it is made, and be comparable with every other discount approval.

| Element | What it specifies | Example: discount approval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | Who is accountable for the class and its template | Head of revenue operations |
| Template | The fields every decision in the class records | Deal size, discount, reason, approver, expected effect |
| Needs list | What a good decision must have considered | Margin floor, competitor price evidence, renewal terms |
| Falsifier convention | How "this was wrong" is defined, and when it is checked | Customer churns or downgrades within 12 months |
| Precedent rule | Which prior decisions count as comparable | Same segment, deal size within 30%, last 18 months |

Kahneman's prescription for noise points the same way: where a formula is not feasible, give people procedures that structure their judgment so similar cases are treated alike. A shared template and needs list is that procedure. Our piece on [the deal desk](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-deal-desk/) shows how one commercial class is usually run at this size.

## Precedent for managers

The single most valuable feature at this stage is the precedent slot: before a manager decides, the three most comparable prior decisions in that class, with outcomes. It gives a new team lead the benefit of the decisions their predecessors made, without needing the predecessors.

Precedent only works if decisions in the class were recorded the same way, which is why the classes come first. With a consistent template, finding the three closest prior cases is a straightforward retrieval task. Our explainer [*What is decision precedent in AI?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) covers how assistants can surface it, and why the outcome field matters more than the summary.

## Handovers become routine

With regular departures and internal moves, handovers happen most months. Make the five-part handover pack standard for any role that owns decisions.

| Part | What it contains |
| --- | --- |
| Decisions | The open and recent decisions the role owns, with reasons and falsifier dates |
| Open threads | Commitments in progress, with the next action and its date |
| Relationships | The people inside and outside the firm who matter, and the state of each |
| Graveyard | What was tried and abandoned, and why, so it is not retried blindly |
| Question log | What the outgoing person was asked most, and the answers |

It is the cheapest protection against losing reasoning when people move. On the commercial line, the same idea applies to deals moving from sales to delivery, covered in [*The handover from sales to delivery*](https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/).

## The first calibration

Pick the highest-volume class with outcomes that arrive within two quarters, often sales deals or renewals, and add a probability to each decision. After a year you will know, for the first time, whether the organisation's judgment in that class is well calibrated, and whose calls are reliable.

The forecasting research supports the effort. Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues, summarising the Good Judgment Project, report that training in probabilistic reasoning helps, that teams forecast significantly better than individuals working alone, and that well-designed aggregation of forecasts beat the simple average by as much as 60%. None of that is possible without a recorded probability and a recorded outcome. Our piece [*Calibration is the honest learning signal*](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) sets out the method.

## The trap: compliance theatre

The trap at two hundred is compliance theatre. Templates get longer, fields multiply, and people fill them to satisfy the process rather than to record their thinking. Hold the line on the three-field floor: decision, reason, what would change your mind. Draft the rest. Measure capture time and keep it under a minute.

**In practice:** define the ten most common decision classes with owner, template, needs list and falsifier convention. Add a precedent slot to the workflow for each class. Make the handover pack mandatory for any role that owns decisions. Start calibration in one high-volume class with short outcome lag. Audit capture time quarterly, and cut any field that is not used.

**What would prove this wrong:** two-hundred-person organisations without structured decision classes or precedent showing no more inconsistency in similar decisions, and no slower manager ramp-up, than those with them. A noise audit in one class is the cheapest way to find out. The next rung, [*One thousand people: governance arrives*](https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/), is where outsiders start asking to see the record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume inconsistency until measured.** Run a small noise audit in one class before arguing about it.
- **Formalise the classes.** Owner, template, needs list and falsifier convention for the ten most common.
- **Show precedent before the decision.** Three comparable prior cases, with outcomes.
- **Standardise handovers.** Decisions, open threads, relationships, graveyard and question log.
- **Guard the floor.** Three required fields, everything else drafted, capture under a minute.

## Next move

Pick one recurring decision class, give five recent cases to three managers who did not decide them, and compare their answers. The spread tells you whether to formalise that class first.
